hints: Focus on what volatility really means, how easily molecules escape the liquid to become gas, which depends on forces between molecules, not inside them.
Notice that $Q_2$ molecules like $Cl_2$, $Br_2$ and $I_2$ are perfectly non-polar, so they cannot have permanent dipole forces, only temporary London forces.
Consider how a bigger atom with many more electrons down the group is more easily polarised, making those temporary dipoles stronger and the substance less volatile.
walkthrough:
**Link volatility to intermolecular forces**

Think of volatility as how easily molecules break free from each other. Stronger forces between molecules means less volatility, higher boiling point.

Rule to remember:
$$\text{stronger intermolecular forces} \rightarrow \text{lower volatility}$$

**Identify the forces in $Q_2$**

$Cl_2$, $Br_2$ and $I_2$ are non-polar diatomic molecules. The two identical atoms share electrons equally, so there is no permanent dipole.

That leaves only one type of force between molecules:
$$\text{instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (London dispersion) forces}$$

**Explain the trend down Group 17**

Going down from Cl to Br to I, each molecule has more electrons and a larger, more diffuse electron cloud. The cloud is more polarisable, so larger temporary dipoles form more easily.

In short:
$$\text{more electrons} \rightarrow \text{stronger London forces} \rightarrow \text{less volatile}$$ 
This is why chlorine is a gas, bromine is a volatile liquid and iodine is a solid.

**Check why the other facts do not explain it**

It is true that Q-Q bond energy and first ionisation energy decrease down the group, but those describe breaking a covalent bond or removing an electron. Volatility only breaks the weak forces between $Q_2$ molecules, leaving the $Q_2$ molecules intact.

options.A: Correct. Volatility decreases down Group 17 because London (instantaneous dipole-induced dipole) forces get stronger with more electrons and greater polarisability, so more energy is needed to separate the $Q_2$ molecules.
options.B: False. $Q_2$ molecules are non-polar because both atoms are identical, so there is no permanent dipole moment. This is a common trap of confusing polar bonds with polar molecules.
options.C: False. The Q-Q covalent bond energy does generally decrease down the group, but volatility does not break covalent bonds. It only overcomes intermolecular forces, so this true statement does not explain the trend.
options.D: False. First ionisation energy $Q(g) \rightarrow Q^+(g) + e^-$ does decrease down the group due to increased shielding and distance, but forming gaseous ions has nothing to do with boiling a simple molecular substance.
